title: Update on ICU and Hospital Capacity
what_it_is: Update on ICU and Hospital Capacity

sections.label: COVID-19 hospital and ICU occupancy
sections.summary: 1,672 COVID-19 patients occupy about 18% of acute public hospital beds, with 284 needing oxygen and 130 critically ill in ICU.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: As of yesterday, we have 1,672 COVID-19 patients admitted into our acute hospitals and they take up about 18% of hospital beds in our acute public hospitals.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: The occupancy rate of all our general ward beds is currently at about 90%.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: Of the COVID-19 patients who are hospitalised, the more serious cases will need oxygen supplementation.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: This number of cases continues to increase, with 284 cases currently needing oxygen support in the general wards.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: Even though this is a small proportion, it translates into a large absolute number of ICU patients when case numbers are high and will place a serious strain on our ICU capacity.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: There are currently 130 patients who are critically ill in the ICU.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: All of these patients require the continuous care of the ICU team.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: They occupy around 60% of the 219 ICU beds currently reserved for COVID-19 patients.

sections.label: Expanding COVID-19 beds and ICU capacity
sections.summary: Sick leave is no longer used as a work performance indicator, and COVID-19 treatment facility and ICU bed capacity is being expanded.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: To Dr Tan Wu Meng's question about hospital departments factoring in sick leave as one of the indicators of work performance, there have previously been isolated incidents, but this practice has ceased.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: Besides addressing the issues of manpower, we have also been working with public, community and private hospitals to set aside more beds for COVID-19 patients.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: We have also stood up COVID-19 Treatment Facilities (CTFs), which have close to 2,000 beds with an occupancy of 50% or less.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: We are continuing to add further capacity to our CTFs, with a view to reach around 4,000 beds in November.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: We will expand our ICU capacity further, in preparation for a potential rise in severe cases.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: We are currently working with our hospitals to ramp up from 219 to 280 ICU beds for COVID-19 patients.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: If needed, our next expansion will be to 350 beds.

sections.label: Peak COVID-19 ICU cases
sections.summary: At its peak, there were 171 COVID-19 cases in ICU.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: At its peak, we had 171 COVID-19 cases in ICU.

sections.label: COVID-19 fatalities kept low
sections.summary: Fatalities have been kept very low, but 407 deaths have been seen so far.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: We have also managed to keep our fatalities very low.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: But sadly, we have seen 407 deaths so far.

sections.label: Deaths among seniors and unvaccinated
sections.summary: Close to 95% of those who died in the last six months were seniors aged 60 and above, and 72% of all deceased cases were not fully vaccinated.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: Close to 95% of those who died in the last six months were seniors aged 60 and above, and 72% of all deceased cases had not been fully vaccinated.

sections.label: Unvaccinated seniors' higher risk
sections.summary: Unvaccinated people aged 60 and above are six times more likely to need oxygen, eight times more likely to need ICU and 17 times more likely to die.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: Compared to the vaccinated, someone who is 60 years old and above and unvaccinated, is six times more likely to need oxygen, eight times more likely to become critically ill and need the ICU and 17 times more likely to die.

sections.label: COVID-19 deaths versus influenza deaths
sections.summary: The absolute number of COVID-19 deaths will rise over time, perhaps 2,000 a year, compared with about 4,000 annual pre-COVID-19 respiratory deaths.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: But it does mean that over time, the absolute number of deaths from COVID-19 will rise despite the best possible medical care.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: We could have, perhaps, 2,000 deaths per year from COVID-19.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: In comparison, every year, in peacetime, pre-COVID-19, about 4,000 patients pass on as a result of influenza, viral pneumonias and other respiratory diseases.

sections.label: Proper care for infected patients
sections.summary: Everyone infected with COVID-19 must receive proper medical care and the best chance to fight the disease, without excess mortality so far.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: We must make sure that everyone who is infected with COVID-19 will receive proper medical care by our healthcare workers and hospital system and be given the best possible chance to fight the disease.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: We have got to this point in our fight against COVID-19 without excess mortality.

sections.label: High vaccination and boosting in Singapore
sections.summary: Singapore aims, unlike any other country, to combine high vaccination, booster jabs and mild infections so COVID-19 no longer spreads as an epidemic.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: What we are trying to do has not yet been done by any other country.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: We are trying to get to the point where the combination of high vaccination rates, booster jabs and even more boosting from mild infections means that COVID-19 will no longer spread as an epidemic in Singapore.

sections.label: No more overall deaths than normal
sections.summary: There will be COVID-19 fatalities, but overall deaths will not exceed those of a normal non-COVID-19 year.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: In other words, though we will have fatalities as a result of COVID-19, we will not see more overall deaths than we would in a normal non-COVID-19 year.

sections.label: Keeping deaths as low as possible
sections.summary: While getting there, the number of deaths should be kept as low as possible, with hope of one of the world's lowest case fatality rates.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: But in getting there we should try to keep the number of deaths as low as possible.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: That we got to this point, where after nearly two years of fighting a pandemic, I can explain our hope to maintain one of the lowest case fatality rates in the world, is a small miracle.

sections.label: Limits of vaccination-differentiated measures
sections.summary: It is not thought possible to go much further than today with vaccination-differentiated measures.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: The question is, how far can we go and we do not think we can go much further than where we are today, with vaccination-differentiated measures.

sections.label: Compulsory vaccination considerations
sections.summary: Making vaccination compulsory is difficult to execute, and factors include vaccination coverage, international practice and vaccine availability and performance.

sentences.speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
sentences.text: The second supplementary question is regarding the Senior Minister of State's observation about the immense stress and pressure on our healthcare workers and what they are shouldering, especially over the last past few months.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: We would have to consider a number of factors: vaccination coverage, international practice and the availability or performance of fully registered COVID-19 vaccines.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: The introduction of the vaccination-differentiated measures, in a way, is to try and get around some of that problem, to expose the different segments of the population to different risks.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: But in terms of making vaccination compulsory, it is also quite difficult in terms of the execution.

sections.label: Benefit and complications
sections.summary: The matter is something to consider, but there are many complications associated with it.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: And the question is, how much benefit will there be?

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: So, I think it is something to consider but there are a whole lot of complications associated with that.

sections.label: Monetary award for healthcare workers
sections.summary: A monetary award is being seriously looked into to recognise healthcare workers' commitment, dedication and physical, mental and emotional stress.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: So, I know that monetary award is not everything but I think it is probably appropriate and the least we can do to recognise their commitment, their dedication and all the physical, mental, emotional stress that they are going through.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: It is something that we are seriously looking into.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: It is carrying a Straits Times article on ICU capacity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: This is dated 13 August and I think this number has been quoted by individuals online as well as when the Minister for Health said that up to 1,000 ICU beds can be made available for critically ill COVID-19 patients, if needed.

sections.label: Healthcare recruitment numbers question
sections.summary: The question asks for recruitment numbers over the same period as the resignations in the healthcare system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: My third question really – and this is the last one, Mr Speaker – follows up on the numbers the Senior Minister of State shared with regard to the resignations in the healthcare system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: One thousand five hundred for the first half of 2021 and I believe an additional 500 were foreign healthcare professionals.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Can I just confirm what have been the recruitment numbers over the same period?

sections.label: F&B industry timing
sections.summary: The F&B industry and families getting together are important, but the time is not here yet.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: It is important to the F&B industry, it is important to Singaporeans, it is important for families to get together.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: But I think the time is not here yet.

sections.label: Augmenting manpower in ICUs
sections.summary: Recruited manpower will augment areas of lower acuity and complexity, and is a medium-term strategy rather than an urgent fix.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: It is going to be augmenting manpower where, perhaps, that level of acuity and that level of complexity does not exist.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: So, while we are recruiting – and we have been actively and I will get the numbers – operationally, I cannot see that that is going to make a huge difference in the ICUs.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: We hope that can displace a little bit of the manpower into some of the higher acuity areas and then release a few people to go and help in the ICU.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: But I think this is a bit more of a medium-term strategy rather than something that we can rely on as an urgent fix to our current problem.

sections.label: Equipment stocks for COVID-19 patients
sections.summary: The system has stocks of equipment, consumables, parts and drugs to cater for many more patients than today.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: If you need the equipment and, thankfully, as a system over the last two years – but it started long before the last two years, through emergency planning and resilience preparedness – we actually have the stocks of equipment that we need: the consumables, the little parts to drive the machines as well as the drugs, in order to cater for many, many more patients than we have today.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: So, as the colleague of mine said, we are not resource-constrained at the moment.

sections.label: Daily death numbers changing
sections.summary: The number of deaths is dynamic, with 13 yesterday and 14 the day before, compared to two to four at end-September.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: So, the number is something that we have to think about in a fairly dynamic way.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
sentences.text: We had 13 yesterday, 14 the day before; 16, 15, 10, as compared to the end of September, where the deaths were two, three, four.

sections.label: Risk of dying unchanged
sections.summary: The proportion of COVID-19 patients needing ICU and dying has not changed, but absolute total numbers are rising for two reasons.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: Of people who get COVID-19, the risk of dying, the proportion of them who go on to need the ICU and then, subsequently succumbed actually has not changed.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: There are two major reasons why we are starting to see the absolute total numbers rise now.

sections.label: Deaths not same as infections
sections.summary: The deaths being seen now are not necessarily the same people infected this week.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: The deaths that we are seeing now are not necessarily the same people who are being infected this week.

sections.label: ICU beds per population
sections.summary: Before the discussion on increasing COVID-19 coverage to 1,000 ICU beds, ICU beds per 100,000 population was about six.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: I have two questions to follow up on pre-empting infrastructure.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: I would note that just before this discussion about increasing COVID-19 coverage to 1,000 ICU beds, our ICU beds per 100,000 population was about six.

sections.label: Global nurse shortage estimates
sections.summary: WHO estimates nine million nurses needed worldwide by 2030, and 370,000 for the US.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Given the global nurse shortage, WHO actually estimates that by 2030, there will be nine million needed worldwide and 370,000 just for the US.

sections.label: ICU clinical outcomes comparison
sections.summary: The speaker says ICU and healthcare clinical outcomes are more than comparable to listed countries, with perhaps fewer total beds per population.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: I think what we are most interested in is what the ICU system and the healthcare system is able to deliver in terms of clinical outcomes.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: I think if the Member dove into those details, he would find that our clinical outcomes and our ICU outcomes are much more than comparable to any of those countries that he has listed, with perhaps less total beds per population.

sections.label: Nurse cross-training and deployment
sections.summary: The speaker says cross-training and cross-deployment of nurses and reduction of elective work to free resources were concerted efforts during the lull.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: As I had explained, the cross-training and the cross deployment of nurses, that was a concerted effort.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: The reduction in elective work to free up resources, that was a concerted effort during the lull.

sections.label: ICU bed capacity and utilisation
sections.summary: The speaker says 382 total ICU beds exist, with 163 non-COVID-19 ICU beds at 80% utilisation, up from 63% pre-COVID-19.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: It would have been a waste of resources but it also would not have been effective in terms of changing the outcomes currently.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: I stress again that while the healthcare system is under stress and our healthcare workers are tired, they are delivering excellent outcomes.

sentences.speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
sentences.text: I have a supplementary question related to ICU bed capacity.

sentences.speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
sentences.text: I have a question because based on the data provided, we have currently, I think, 382 total ICU beds and he also said that 163 non-COVID-19 ICU beds are running at 80% utilisation today, an increase from 63% pre-COVID-19.

sections.label: Impact acknowledged
sections.summary: The speaker says there is firstly an impact.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: Actually, I would say, firstly there is an impact.

sections.label: ICU beds on standby load
sections.summary: The speaker says about 160 ICU beds are set aside for non-COVID-19 patients and 280 for COVID-19 patients, creating a logistical and administrative load of about 140% to 145% compared to peacetime.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: So, when you had 100 ICU beds, you may have 60% occupancy; now, we have got 280 ICU beds, you are still at 60% occupancy.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: So, it sounds as if it is not too much of an issue, but if we try to think of it in terms of workload; so, currently, we have about 160 ICU beds set aside for non-COVID-19 patients.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: There is an administrative and logistical load keeping those beds on standby.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: We also have, by the end of this week, 280 beds set aside for COVID-19 patients in the ICU.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: So, 440 beds, currently set aside in ICU.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: It is exactly 298, but let us say 300; so, essentially, the hospital system is carrying a logistical and administrative load of about 140%, 145% compared to peacetime, just on standby.

sections.label: Pre-COVID ICU patient numbers
sections.summary: The speaker says pre-COVID-19 in 2019 the hospital system averaged about 180 ICU patients across the landscape.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: Pre-COVID-19, 2019, we had about on average in the hospital system 180 ICU patients across the across the landscape.

sections.label: Sinovac preference and mRNA recommendation
sections.summary: Few prefer or need Sinovac, its Delta effectiveness is not demonstrated like other vaccines, so mRNA vaccines are recommended.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: For Sinovac, I think we have to remember that the proportion of people who prefer Sinovac and who need Sinovac is very, very small.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: It is 1% or 2% of our total base.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: But also that its effectiveness with the Delta variant has not been demonstrated to the same degree as all the other vaccines.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: With our national vaccination programme, if you get the infection even though you have had the vaccination, having had the vaccination converts it to a mild illness, a mild illness you may not even be aware of, an asymptomatic infection and, potentially, rest at home as a result.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: We do not have such data for Sinovac and so, given that is the case, we feel it is our clinical responsibility to recommend that if it is possible, our population take the mRNA vaccine.

sections.label: Oxygen cases and ICU projection
sections.summary: Not all oxygen-requiring patients need ICU care, but some will deteriorate, so forward ICU projections affect decisions to loosen measures.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: Not all of them require ICU care but you cannot entirely predict which of them will end up requiring ICU care.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: So, if we have a very large base of people requiring oxygen, you have to be ready that some of them will deteriorate and so there is a forward projection for ICU care that we have to take into account in terms of our decisions to open up or loosen or lighten.

sections.label: Unvaccinated seniors and younger adults
sections.summary: The unvaccinated group includes 70,000 seniors, down from 200,000 in August, and 240,000 relatively healthy people aged 13 to 59 who chose not to be vaccinated.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Because the unvaccinated group consists of: one, the 70,000 seniors who are still unvaccinated and probably, like just now, one of the Members had raised the issue, maybe we should isolate them a bit more, or rather pay attention specially to them so that we cut down on their infection rate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: But these 70,000 had come down from 200,000 in August.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: So, we have to isolate them and special care has to be given to them and more volunteers may be assigned to look after them and all that.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: But there is also another group of unvaccinated people in our country, 240,000 of them, between 13 years old and 59 years old, relatively healthy, but they chosed not to be vaccinated for various reasons.

sections.label: Justifying vaccine-differentiated measures
sections.summary: Unvaccinated people above 60 are 17 times more likely to pass, justifying vaccine-differentiated measures as trying to save their lives and families.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: If you are above the age of 60, you are 17 times more likely to pass, if you are unvaccinated than if you are vaccinated.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: So, a vaccination answers Mr Leong's second question.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: Hence, when he then asks, "How do we justify our vaccine-differentiated measures and how do we justify imposing something on people who chose not to get vaccinated?" Our justification is that we are trying to save their lives, we are trying for their loved ones and their family not to lose a family member.

sections.label: Human-to-human infection route
sections.summary: The route of infection is largely from human-to-human contact.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: The route of infection is largely from human-to-human contact.

sections.label: Hospital backlog and healthcare worker leave
sections.summary: The pandemic caused a backlog of follow-up visits and elective operations, and 90% of healthcare workers could not clear annual leave, prompting a question on hospital plans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
sentences.text: According to the Director of Medical Services, the COVID-19 pandemic has caused a significant backlog of follow-up visits and elective operations, and it will take the hospitals many months to catch up and clear this backlog.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
sentences.text: The Senior Minister of State also earlier mentioned that 90% of our healthcare workers were not able to clear their annual leave.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
sentences.text: As there are clear challenges mentioned by the Senior Minister of State to quickly increase staffing to alleviate the manpower situation, what are the hospitals planning to do to allow our healthcare professionals to at least take a break during this period?

sections.label: Healthcare staff rest during COVID-19
sections.summary: It is uncertain how long COVID-19 pressure on healthcare will last, so teams will use rotating leave patterns to give staff rest.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: We are also uncertain how long this will go on for, so it is a bit hard to predict where we will be in terms of this – the rest of the healthcare system's duties and responsibilities once COVID-19 starts to wane – because we do not quite know when that will happen.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: So, there is a stress on the healthcare system, it will persist for some time after COVID-19 starts to come down, precisely for the reasons the Member has identified.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: But the hospitals and the staff, the leadership are going to try to find ways to give their teams some rest and I do not think this is something that we can settle on a policy basis, it is very granular, it depends on the size of your team and the various other duties, when is your lull time, when is your up time.

sentences.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
sentences.text: And I suspect what will happen is that the different teams, the different departments, the different divisions will allow rotating leave in different patterns to suit their acuity levels.

sections.label: Sinovac option for seniors
sections.summary: Sinovac is available under the National Vaccination Programme in some clinics and at Raffles City Vaccination Centre for those 60 and above who cannot or do not want mRNA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: As the Senior Minister of State mentioned, it is now available as an option under our National Vaccination Programme.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: So, it is generally available in some clinics and also at the Raffles City Vaccination Centre just nearby.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: So, if you are 60 and above, cannot take or just do not want to take mRNA, you can walk in to take your Sinovac.

sections.label: Nursing home and household infection rates
sections.summary: Nursing home infections are about 6.4% of total senior infections, and about 10% of household members get infected after a positive case.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: Nursing home infections are a small percentage of the total senior infection.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: The last I calculated, it is not the most updated but it is about 6.4%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: Within a household, if somebody is positive, approximately 10% of household members will subsequently get infected.
